8: export class DisjointSets {
9:   #parent;
10:   #size;
11:   #components;
12: 
13:   /**
14:    * @param {number} count How many elements the structure holds.
15:    */
16:   constructor(count) {
17:     this.#parent = Array.from({ length: count }, (_, index) => index);
18:     this.#size = new Array(count).fill(1);
19:     this.#components = count;
20:   }
21: 
22:   /** @returns {number} How many elements the structure holds. */
23:   get count() {
24:     return this.#parent.length;
25:   }
26: 
27:   /** @returns {number} How many disjoint sets exist right now. */
28:   get components() {
29:     return this.#components;
30:   }
31: 
32:   /**
33:    * Finds the representative of an element's set.
34:    * @param {number} element Element to look up.
35:    * @returns {number} Root element of the set.
36:    */
37:   find(element) {
38:     let node = element;
39:     while (this.#parent[node] !== node) node = this.#parent[node];
40:     for (let step = element; this.#parent[step] !== node; ) {
41:       const next = this.#parent[step];
42:       this.#parent[step] = node;
43:       step = next;
44:     }
45:     return node;
46:   }
47: 
48:   /**
49:    * Reports whether two elements share a set.
50:    * @param {number} a First element.
51:    * @param {number} b Second element.
52:    * @returns {boolean} True when both share a representative.
53:    */
54:   connected(a, b) {
55:     return this.find(a) === this.find(b);
56:   }
57: 
58:   /**
59:    * Reports how many elements share an element's set.
60:    * @param {number} element Element to measure.
61:    * @returns {number} Size of the set.
62:    */
63:   sizeOf(element) {
64:     return this.#size[this.find(element)];
65:   }
66: 
67:   /**
68:    * Joins two sets, attaching the smaller under the larger and, on a tie, the
69:    * larger root index under the smaller.
70:    * @param {number} a First element.
71:    * @param {number} b Second element.
72:    * @returns {boolean} False when both elements already shared a set.
73:    */
74:   union(a, b) {
75:     const rootA = this.find(a);
76:     const rootB = this.find(b);
77:     if (rootA === rootB) return false;
78:     const root = this.#size[rootB] > this.#size[rootA] ? rootB : rootA;
79:     const attached = root === rootA ? rootB : rootA;
80:     this.#parent[attached] = root;
81:     this.#size[root] += this.#size[attached];
82:     this.#components -= 1;
83:     return true;
84:   }

105:    * @returns {number} How many unions were undone.
106:    */
107:   rollback(token) {

109:   }

111:   /**
112:    * Lists the sets, each sorted ascending, ordered by their smallest member.
113:    * @returns {number[][]} Current partition.
114:    */
115:   groups() {
116:     /** @type {Map<number, number[]>} */
117:     const byRoot = new Map();
118:     for (let element = 0; element < this.#parent.length; element += 1) {

Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. 5: /** Deterministic 32-bit PRNG so generated command sequences replay identically. */

**Summary of what was implemented:**

  2. Replay check via a `commandId → result` map (returns cached result with `replayed: true`, no audit entry, no state change)
  3. Clock regression check (`CLOCK_REGRESSION`, audit stamped with current clock)
  4. State-machine guard (`BAD_STATE`)
  5. Field checks (`MISSING_FIELD`, `BAD_AMOUNT`)
  6. Business guards (`DUPLICATE_SKU`, `NO_SUCH_ITEM`, `EMPTY_ORDER`, `AMOUNT_MISMATCH`, `REFUND_TOO_LARGE`)
  7. Effect application + audit entry (`from`/`to`/`ok`/optional `code`)

goal.objective:
Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `tokenize`, `parse`, `evaluate` and the error class `ExprError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `tokenize(input)` returns tokens in source order, each `{ type, value, index }` where `index` is the 0-based position in UTF-16 code units. Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. Evaluation reports `division by zero at 1` for `/` or `%` with a zero divisor, and `non-finite result at 5` whenever an operation or call produces something that is not a finite number, each pointing at the operator or the call's name.

`evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. The callable functions are fixed: `abs`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties toward positive infinity), `sign` take exactly one argument; `pow` and `atan2` take exactly two; `min` and `max` take one or more. Calling anything else throws `unknown function: foo at 0`, and a wrong count throws `function abs expects 1 argument, got 2 at 0`, `function pow expects 2 arguments, got 1 at 0` or `function max expects at least 1 argument, got 0 at 0`. 5: /** Deterministic 32-bit PRNG so generated command sequences replay identically. */
6: function mulberry32(seed) {
7:   let a = seed >>> 0;
8:   return function next() {
9:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
10:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
11:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
12:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
13:   };
14: }

16: /** Build the happy-path order used by several cases. */
17: function deliveredOrder() {
18:   const order = new Order({ id: 'o-1', createdAt: 100 });
19:   order.apply({ type: 'addItem', commandId: 'c1', at: 100, sku: 'apple', qty: 2, unitPriceCents: 150 });
20:   order.apply({ type: 'addItem', commandId: 'c2', at: 101, sku: 'pear', qty: 1, unitPriceCents: 300 });
21:   order.apply({ type: 'pay', commandId: 'c3', at: 102, amountCents: 600 });
22:   order.apply({ type: 'pack', commandId: 'c4', at: 103 });
23:   order.apply({ type: 'ship', commandId: 'c5', at: 104, carrier: 'ups', tracking: 'zz9' });
24:   order.apply({ type: 'deliver', commandId: 'c6', at: 105 });
25:   return order;
26: }
27: 
28: test('construction validates its identity and clock', () => {
29:   assert.throws(() => new Order(null), { name: 'TypeError', message: 'init must be an object' });
30:   assert.throws(() => new Order({ id: '' }), { name: 'TypeError', message: 'init.id must be a non-empty string' });
31:   assert.throws(() => new Order({ id: 'o', createdAt: -1 }), { name: 'TypeError' });
32:   assert.throws(() => new Order({ id: 'o', createdAt: 1.5 }), { name: 'TypeError' });
33:   const order = new Order({ id: 'o' });
34:   assert.equal(order.id, 'o');
35:   assert.equal(order.state, 'created');
36:   assert.equal(order.clockMs, 0);
37:   assert.deepEqual(order.snapshot(), {
38:     id: 'o',
39:     state: 'created',
40:     items: [],
41:     totalCents: 0,
42:     paidCents: 0,
43:     refundedCents: 0,
44:     clockMs: 0,

50:   const order = new Order({ id: 'o' });

53:     name: 'TypeError',

Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. It throws `'NOT_FOUND'` with message `unknown entry: <id>` for an unknown entry, `'REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL'` when the target is itself a reversal, `'ALREADY_REVERSED'` with message `entry already reversed: <id>` for a second reversal, and `'BAD_TIME'` when the reversal would precede its entry; a reversal that fails to post leaves the original untouched. `statement(accountId, { from, to })` lists the account's lines inside an inclusive window as `{ entryId, at, seq, amountCents, balanceCents }`, ordered like `entries()`, where `balanceCents` is the running balance counting everything from the beginning of the ledger, not just the window. goal.objective:
Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

content.text:
`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

  "prompt": "`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.\n\nParsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.\n\n`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.\n\nA string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`.",

goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. It throws `'NOT_FOUND'` with message `unknown entry: <id>` for an unknown entry, `'REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL'` when the target is itself a reversal, `'ALREADY_REVERSED'` with message `entry already reversed: <id>` for a second reversal, and `'BAD_TIME'` when the reversal would precede its entry; a reversal that fails to post leaves the original untouched. `statement(accountId, { from, to })` lists the account's lines inside an inclusive window as `{ entryId, at, seq, amountCents, balanceCents }`, ordered like `entries()`, where `balanceCents` is the running balance counting everything from the beginning of the ledger, not just the window. goal.objective:
Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. It throws `'NOT_FOUND'` with message `unknown entry: <id>` for an unknown entry, `'REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL'` when the target is itself a reversal, `'ALREADY_REVERSED'` with message `entry already reversed: <id>` for a second reversal, and `'BAD_TIME'` when the reversal would precede its entry; a reversal that fails to post leaves the original untouched. `statement(accountId, { from, to })` lists the account's lines inside an inclusive window as `{ entryId, at, seq, amountCents, balanceCents }`, ordered like `entries()`, where `balanceCents` is the running balance counting everything from the beginning of the ledger, not just the window. Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected.
